scenario_stem:
Country X Broadcasting Corporation (CXBC) is a public corporation owned and funded by the State of Country X. Established in 1988, it employs 2,400 staff and runs 4 television channels and 6 radio stations. Last year it received $95 million in licence fees and a state grant of $30 million, yet its annual report showed a deficit of $12 million after spending $18 million on new digital transmitters.

The government proposes selling CXBC to Halcyon Media, a private media group, for $180 million, arguing the sale would fund a $140 million digital switchover programme. Broadcasting unions fear the buyer would cut 3 regional news services, axe 350 jobs and chase advertising revenue with cheaper entertainment. CXBC's board insists it is fulfilling its public service remit, providing educational and cultural programmes watched by 6 million viewers a week.

Reason 2: To keep broadcasting affordable and impartial [k], last year it received a $30 million state grant alongside licence fees rather than relying on advertising revenue alone [app].

The service employs 130 refuse collectors and 18 supervisors and operates a fleet of 22 lorries. Last year it collected 96,000 tonnes of waste and cost $9.4 million to run. The fleet is ageing, with 6 lorries now over 12 years old, and breakdowns rose by 40% in 3 years.

The council is considering a 7-year contract worth $58 million with Sycamore Environmental Services, a private waste firm. Sycamore promises annual savings of $1.6 million, 8 electric lorries and a 98% on-time collection rate. It operates 28 aircraft serving 45 routes, employs 3,600 staff and carried 4.8 million passengers last year. The Country X National Theatre (CXNT) is a public corporation staging drama, opera and dance in the capital. Founded in 1954, it employs 340 staff and received $38 million in government funding last year, covering 62% of its costs, with ticket sales covering the remaining 38%. Some 900,000 people attended performances. Four of its 9 productions toured regional theatres, reaching 40,000 schoolchildren.

The culture minister proposes selling CXNT to Aurora Stage Group, a private theatre company, for $75 million, arguing taxpayers should not fund the arts. CXNT's board warns the buyer would scrap the regional touring programme, end the 40,000-pupil education scheme and favour popular musicals to maximise profit. Average ticket prices would likely rise from $28 to $40 per seat, and 90 staff could be made redundant.
